title: Ardas in grief
hookLine: the Ardas for the dead asks peace for the one who has gone, and for those left, the strength to accept the Will

lines: A FAMILY, A FEW DAYS AFTER.
cards: A family stands in a gurdwara a few days after a funeral. Some of them haven't slept. Someone holds a framed photo; someone else holds a toddler who doesn't understand why everyone is so quiet.
In the days since the death, the Guru Granth Sahib has been read, perhaps from beginning to end. Now the reading is finished. The congregation rises, and the Ardas begins.
Somewhere in it, the name of the one who died is spoken aloud, for the last time in this way.

teach.b: Sikhs usually cremate their dead, and Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns, is sung at the cremation.
Over the following days, families often hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, and when it ends, an Ardas is said that is often called the antim ardas, the final prayer. It asks two things.

teach.h: REST FOR THE ONE WHO HAS GONE.
teach.b: For the one who has gone: that their soul find rest, a place at the Guru's feet, union with the One. And for the ones left: the strength to accept the Will.
That word, will, is bhaana, and it runs all through Sikh teaching. Bhaana mannan, accepting the Will, is honored, and it is hard. Guru Arjan put it in a single line.
In Raag Asa, on ang 394, he says, in effect: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. An honest note. Accepting the Will doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt.
Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing and ritual displays of mourning, and treats death as part of the One's order rather than a punishment. But it doesn't forbid tears.
Acceptance is something people grow into, sometimes over years, and the Ardas doesn't demand it be finished by Sunday; it asks for the strength to keep moving toward it.
And the family isn't asked to do this alone. The whole congregation stands with them, and the line rising spirits, good for all, is said even here.

how: After a death, Sikhs sing Kirtan Sohila at the cremation, often hold a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and close it with an Ardas asking rest for the departed and acceptance of the Will for the family.

o: the Will of the One, to be accepted
the final reading of the scripture
a prayer said for the dead at a funeral

p: the final prayer after the reading
what You do seems sweet to me

s: accepting the Will means never crying
Sikh teaching discourages wailing displays, but it doesn't forbid tears; acceptance takes time.
with Kirtan Sohila sung at the cremation.
the Ardas in grief prays only for the family
it asks rest for the one who has gone and strength for those left.

games.q: the reading is finished, the family stands for the Ardas. what does it ask for the ones left behind?
o: the strength to accept the Will.
games.why: bhaana mannan, accepting the Will: hard, honored, and something people grow into.

practice: Take this at whatever depth feels right today: bring to mind someone you miss, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, or someone who isn't gone but is far away, and if it hurts, let it hurt a little. Breathe.
If you pray, you can ask peace for them, and the strength to accept what you can't change, with a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Bhaana, the Will of the One: after a death, the Ardas asks rest for the one who has gone, and for the family, the strength to accept it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Will of the One; bhaana mannan, accepting it.

carryVoice: Your line: in his will. Acceptance can take years, and tears are allowed along the way. That's day six hundred forty-one.
